pointOfInterests.description: Apache Falls is a large nearly unrunnable waterfall ledge above the put in for the Salt Canyon run. Running the ledge is illegal.
pointOfInterests.name: Apache Falls

pointOfInterests.description: Island Rapid is a wave train with holes. Unless the river is above 1200 cfs it is best to avoid this rapid by using the normal access point at First Campground which is just downstream of this rapid.
pointOfInterests.name: Island Rapid

pointOfInterests.description: Most boaters use this access point for the put in located on river right just downstream of the Highway 60 Bridge. There are separate launch areas for public use and outfitter use. This is a good place to camp the night before your trip. A small class II rapid, Kiss & Tell, is immediately downstream.
pointOfInterests.name: First Campground Access Point

pointOfInterests.description: Short drop over a cobble bar just downstream of the put in.
pointOfInterests.name: Kiss and Tell

pointOfInterests.description: Short drop over a gravel bar where careful route selection is important at low water to avoid getting stuck.
pointOfInterests.name: Bump and Grind Rapid

pointOfInterests.description: An island divides the flow. The deepest channel is on river right.
pointOfInterests.name: Maytag

pointOfInterests.description: A wave train with a big hole on river left.
pointOfInterests.name: Grumman Rapid

pointOfInterests.description: A big boulder in the center of the channel. The main line is around the right.
pointOfInterests.name: Mother Rock

pointOfInterests.description: A shallow shoal on river left that is best run down a chute to the far right bank.
pointOfInterests.name: Overboard

pointOfInterests.description: This is a designated primitive campground managed by the White Mountain Apache Tribe. It is popular with outfitters during the rafting season for those doing day trips.
pointOfInterests.name: Second Campground River Access

pointOfInterests.description: A big wave train with some great play waves .
pointOfInterests.name: Exhibition Rapid

pointOfInterests.description: This river access point sometimes washes out when Cibecue Creek floods.
pointOfInterests.name: Cibecue Creek Access

pointOfInterests.description: Rapid formed by the outwash from Cibecue Rapid.
pointOfInterests.name: Cibecue Rapid

pointOfInterests.description: The river splits around islands with most of the flow going around to river right.
pointOfInterests.name: Three Way Rapid

pointOfInterests.description: Some boulders to avoid particularly at lower flows.
pointOfInterests.name: Raft Ripper Rapid

pointOfInterests.description: A rock strewn wave train with occasional play holes.
pointOfInterests.name: Mescal Falls

pointOfInterests.description: Unimproved access near the end of the day trip section.
pointOfInterests.name: Mescal River Access

pointOfInterests.description: Unimproved river access and the last option at the end of the day trip section.
pointOfInterests.name: Hoodoo River Access

pointOfInterests.description: A cobble bar pushes most of the flow to the right. The Salt Banks are at the bottom of the rapid on river right where water coming in is very saline forming impressive salt deposits.
pointOfInterests.name: Salt Banks

pointOfInterests.description: Ledges rapid is formed when the river flows over several low angle quartzite ledges. This rapid has some of the best play waves and holes on almost any river.
pointOfInterests.name: Ledges Rapid

pointOfInterests.description: Stay clear of the hydraulic on river left where the river flows over a rock ledge.
pointOfInterests.name: Little Boat Eater

pointOfInterests.description: A number of rocks and features to navigate your way through the "garden."
pointOfInterests.name: Rock Garden Rapid

pointOfInterests.description: A cobble bar rapid that is just above Rat Trap.
pointOfInterests.name: The Cheese Rapid

pointOfInterests.description: A long rapid with big exploding waves and large holes. Rat Trap marks the start of a micro canyon of polished granite. The next 5 miles are reminiscent of California whitewater.
pointOfInterests.name: Rat Trap

pointOfInterests.description: Polished boulers, boiling eddies, irreglar waves and holes are common for the next few miles.
pointOfInterests.name: White Rock Rapid

pointOfInterests.description: Canyon Creek flows into the Salt on river right. This creek can be boated at higher flows. It is a good option for a lunch stop and hike up the drainage.
pointOfInterests.name: Canyon Creek

pointOfInterests.description: Just past the confluence of Canyon Creek, Granite Rapid is probably the largest rapid in the microgorge and marks the final drop before Gleason Flat.
pointOfInterests.name: Granite Rapid

pointOfInterests.description: Gleason Rapid is a minor rapid just upstream of South Gleason River Access. This intermediate access point can be reached by a four-wheel drive access road that enters the canyon off Forest Road 303B. From this point downstream, wilderness permits from the Forest Service are required.
pointOfInterests.name: Gleason Rapid

pointOfInterests.description: The Salt enters another granite microgorge and is pinched down as it flows over a ledge with a powerful hole. Scout on river left.
pointOfInterests.name: Eye of the Needle

pointOfInterests.description: Black Rock is the final rapid in a small micro gorge. The Salt is choked with sharp boulders and drops over some ledges and the preferred line is not readily apparent as the river disappears around the corner to the right. The line changes at different flows, particularly because there are rocks in the water after the ledge that can be partially covered. With enough flow, rafts will typically run river right near a 6' pourover. Kayaks and packrafts have different lines depending on the flow, either dropping off a ledge or following the tongue and punching through the hole river left. Watch out for the boiling froth and then the current pushing hard left up against an undercut rock immediately after the rapid. Rafts scout from far upstream river right, kayaks scout river left.
pointOfInterests.name: Black Rock

pointOfInterests.description: The Salt is split by a huge boulder. Most rafts must run right but hard boats can run slots down the left.
pointOfInterests.name: Devils Pendejo

pointOfInterests.description: Easy rapid with some boulders and cobbles.
pointOfInterests.name: Upper Corral

pointOfInterests.description: A wave train with a huge hole in the center at higher flows. This rapid marks the transition between White Mountain Apache Tribal Lands on river right to the Tonto National Forest.
pointOfInterests.name: Lower Corral

pointOfInterests.description: Pinball has everything from large waves and holes to boiling eddies. Don't swim here or you could wash into Maze, a dangerous rapid.
pointOfInterests.name: Pinball

pointOfInterests.description: Maze is a complex rapid that starts with a pair of big holes on river left and then snakes around a corner toward the right to feed a narrow canyon with boiling eddies. This is not a fun rapid to swim or flip a raft.
pointOfInterests.name: The Maze Rapid

pointOfInterests.description: Quartzite Falls was once the bane of Salt raft trips, a challenging class V rapid. At almost all flows it involved a half day portage and difficult rope work. Those days are gone becuase the falls, as they existed, were destroyed with dyanamite that was used to blow the lower lip off the falls. The rapid is now an easier class IV rapid with a small but shallow hole at the base on river right that can still flip a loaded raft. This once infamous rapid is still one of the "big drops" on the Salt. The traditional scout is reached by stopping well upstream of the rapid and hiking up to the ridge on river left. It's hard to get a good perspective on the drop from this view. Depending on flows, those with good boat control and eddy catching skills can also potentially land just above the drop on river right. A run down the left is possible but a standard line is center right. If you do this line you need to pivot your boat to square up to the lateral that comes in from the right. This lateral can easily flip a loaded raft and you have a short recovery pool before you reach Corkscrew which is another class IV drop just downstream.
pointOfInterests.name: Quartzite Falls

pointOfInterests.description: Corkscrew is still one of the biggest rapids on the Salt. This complicated wave train has huge hole and exploding waves. A swim here can be long and rafts can flip here at higher water. Often boaters forget about Corkscrew in the excitiment of Quartzite Falls. Portage from river left.
pointOfInterests.name: Corkscrew

pointOfInterests.description: An easy line down the right once you pass the hole near the top on the right.
pointOfInterests.name: Sleeper Rapid

pointOfInterests.description: Cliffhanger is an easy shoal with a huge rock in the main flow. The eddy on river left near the big boulder is very difficult to escape in a raft.
pointOfInterests.name: Cliffhanger

pointOfInterests.description: A nice side hike with clean clear water on river right.
pointOfInterests.name: Cherry Creek

pointOfInterests.description: This is a straightfoward gravel bar rapid as the river bends around to the right. It serves as an alternate access point and the launching spot for tubers during the summer.
pointOfInterests.name: Horseshoe Bend

pointOfInterests.description: A minor riffle and the end of the whitewater.
pointOfInterests.name: Redmond Rapid

pointOfInterests.description: Coon Creek is a fun side hike with opportunities for exploration. If you have a few hours you can hike up and over the ridge and then down Dry Creek and Chalk Creek.
pointOfInterests.name: Coon Creek

pointOfInterests.description: Take out on river left just donwstream of the bridge. A nice ramp provides access to the river.
pointOfInterests.name: Highway 288 Takeout

pointOfInterests.description: This 3 foot dam creates a lethal hole. Take out at the bridge before this artificial drop.
pointOfInterests.name: Diversion Dam

alerts.title: Rogue throw bag in Overboard
alerts.detail: On 4/19/2024 we noted a throw bag in Overboard rapid between the big rock at the bottom and the cobblestone shoal on river left. The rope was attached to something in the river left shoal about 75 feet up stream from the bottom pour over. We were able to capture the bag/rope with another throw bag and moved the rope upstream as far as we could to dislodge it from whatever it was connected to but were unable to get it out. After moving into the river above the shoal as far as we could safely go we secured as much of the throw bag and rope that we could and then cut the rope. There is still rope on the far left side near the cobblestone shoal maybe 25ft or less before the large rock at the bottom. It should be out of the main line now and would only present a possible hazard to someone swimming far left near the cobblestone. This should be completely removed when flows lower and allow easier access to the cobblestone bar.

alerts.detail: The road to access the upper canyon is closed and barricaded. No permits are available for sale through the tribe.

alerts.title: NEW! Upper Salt River Portage 2022
alerts.detail: Hundreds of yards long portage currently at Horseshoe Bend. Looks like it would prove very difficult for larger crafts. More info here =>https://www.facebook.com/SaltRiverRafting/posts/10158281460226962

detail.permitInfo: Lottery for river permits Mar 1 through May 15. Applications due Jan 31.
detail.description:
The first part of this run can be done as a day trip before the river leaves the road behind for a wonderful multiday run on the Upper Salt from the Salt River Canyon Bridge on Highway 60 to Roosevelt Reservoir. The trip can be done in as few as 2 days but 4 or 5 days allows for a more relaxed pace and opportunities for hiking. Those doing the multi-day trip have the opportunity to enjoy 30 miles of whitewater in a spectacular Sonoran Desert canyon, followed by a serene 20 mile exit float. For gear-hauling rafts, a minimum flow of 1,200 cfs is recommended. For kayaks and packrafts the rapids are enjoyable down to about 400cfs. The infamous rapid Quartzite is a solid class IV at most levels without the class V consequences that existed at high flows before it was illegally blasted.

A Wilderness permit from Tonto National Forest is required from March 1st to May 15th; the wilderness begins 20 miles downstream from Highway 60. A permit from the White Mountain Apache Tribe is also required for boaters on the upper portion of river flowing through the Reservation which includes the approximately 29-mile stretch of river downstream from First Campground and the Highway 60 Bridge put-in. The Tribe enforces this requirement and it is important that boaters respect their sovereignty and authority.

[Video: Packrafting at 900cfs with rapid names](https://youtu.be/RU0c8d_Is0s?si=T_1ji5HT0hXv9_Bd)

*First Campground (Highway 60) to Hoodoo River Access (9 miles, class III)*

The first 9 miles of the run can be enjoyed as a day trip (with a permit from the Tribe) or the start of a mult-day river trip. There are five class III rapids in this section and several good river camps for those on an overnight trip. Road accessible camps are also available on river right that are typically utilized by those on day trips. Access points on this section include First Campground Access, Cibecue River Access, Mescal River Access, and Hoodoo River Access. These are all located on river right where a lightly used dirt road parallels the run.

*Hoodoo River Access to Roosevelt Reservoir (44 miles, class III-IV)*

The standard multi-day trip begins with the first segment above but once you pass Hoodoo River Access you leave the road behind. The next few days offer incredible Sonoran Desert scenery, several signature rapids, some fun side hikes, and great river camps. The big class IV rapids include Black Rock Rapid, The Maze Rapid, Quartzite Falls, and Corkscrew Rapid that are all in the middle of the run. Shortly after Corkscrew the canyon walls loosen their grip and the river becomes a class II float. Be sure to take-out on river left just below the Highway 288 Bridge. Just downstream the river flows over a dangerous lowhead dam and then enters the slackwater of Roosevelt Reservoir.
